answer.exemplar: A good answer locates the loss precisely, because the conservation law that holds is conservation of total energy and not conservation of mechanical energy. Friction is a non-conservative force, so the work it does depends on the path length and is not recoverable by retracing the path, and the mechanical energy it removes from the block does not disappear. It leaves the mechanical account and enters the internal energy of the two surfaces in contact, which raises their temperature, and part of it also passes into the surroundings as a disturbance in the air. A weak answer says only that it became heat, because that is only half of what has to be shown, namely that the same amount of energy is demonstrably present elsewhere, and an answer that claims the energy vanished contradicts the first law rather than explaining it. A good answer then proposes a measurement that could confirm the account, and the natural one is to measure the temperature rise of the block and the surface and check that the total energy they gained equals the mechanical energy the block lost, which requires measuring the lost mechanical energy as half the mass times the square of the entry speed, since the exit speed is zero. It should note that the two surfaces share the energy in proportion to their heat capacities and thermal conductivities, so the sum rather than either one alone is what must be checked, and a good answer flags the practical difficulty that the temperature rise is tiny and the surfaces are small, so a realistic test uses a long slide and a sensitive thermometer. A strong answer may also note that a block that slides on a lubricated surface still stops, more slowly, and that this is evidence that the loss is proportional to the sliding distance rather than to the time, since the speed decays exponentially with a rate set by the coefficient of friction.

In the resistor the energy is dissipated: the charge carriers are repeatedly deflected by collisions in the material and each collision transfers energy to the lattice, so the energy appears as internal energy of the resistor, that is, as a rise in temperature, and it is not recoverable. The formula that shows the reversibility is the stored energy, half the capacitance times the square of the potential difference, which depends only on the state and not on the route taken to reach it, whereas the dissipated energy, the current squared times the resistance times the time, accumulates in proportion to how long the current flows, and the same current in a longer time dissipates proportionally more. A good answer then states the circuit consequence clearly: a capacitor blocks a steady direct current once charged, because the current is what deposits the charge and there is no longer any voltage to drive it, while a resistor carries a steady current for as long as the voltage is applied and converts the whole of the power into heat continuously. A strong answer adds the consequence for design, since a capacitor is chosen when a circuit must block a frequency or store an amount of energy to be released on demand, and a resistor is chosen when a voltage must be dropped or a current limited, and in both cases the resistance or capacitance value is chosen from a formula that embeds a limit such as a power rating or a working voltage, which are physical constraints rather than mathematical ones. A weak answer gives the two formulas without saying where the energy goes, or claims the capacitor eventually loses its charge on its own, which confuses leakage with dissipation.
